## Recap

Yesterday we learned that we should not take our data for granted!


## Today

### Core idea
> A statistical model is a disciplined comparison.

Today we cover the following:

- How do we choose a statistical test or model?
- How does the outcome type guide the method?
- How can we perform simple robustness and sensitivity checks?


## Terms I may use

- **Comparison**: the contrast that answers the research question
- **Outcome**: the variable we try to describe, explain or predict
- **Predictor / explanatory variable**: the variable that defines the main comparison
- **Covariate / background variable**: a variable used to make the comparison fairer
- **Model**: a structured way to make the comparison
- **Diagnostic**: a check of whether the model behaves reasonably
- **Robustness check**: a check whether the answer survives a reasonable alternative choice
- **Sensitivity check**: a check how much the answer changes when an assumption is varied

## At the start

Let's start with the core:

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
# Modelling
A model is not the answer. A model is the machine that turns a comparison into an answer.
:::

So the first question is not:

> Which test should I use?

The first question is:

> Which comparison would answer my research question?

## The method-first trap

A common mistake:

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
# Method-first thinking
“I want to use regression.”  
“I want to do a t-test.”  
“I want to use a random forest.”
:::

This is backwards.

- A method cannot repair a vague question.
- A complex model cannot repair weak data.
- A significant result cannot repair a poor comparison.

## The analysis route

A more disciplined route:

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
flowchart LR
  A[Research question] --> B[Comparison]
  B --> C[Outcome type]
  C --> D[Data structure]
  D --> E[Method]
  E --> F[Diagnostics]
  F --> G[Claim]
  G --> H[Robustness check]
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
# Rule of thumb
Choose the method after you understand the comparison, the outcome and the data structure.
:::

## What kind of question is it?

| Type question | Central task | Typical output |
|---|---|---|
| **Descriptive** | describe a level, distribution or trend | mean, proportion, table, trend |
| **Comparative** | compare groups or periods | difference in means/proportions |
| **Associational** | relate variables | regression coefficient, odds ratio |
| **Predictive** | predict future or unseen outcomes | prediction error, accuracy |
| **Causal** | estimate effect of intervention/exposure | effect estimate under assumptions |
| **Validation** | compare measurement systems | agreement, calibration, error |

## The same data can support different answers

Imagine a survey on households and water nuisance.

| Question | Possible method | Claim |
|---|---|---|
| How many households report water nuisance? | proportion, table | descriptive |
| Do districts differ? | cross-tab, group comparison | comparative |
| Is water nuisance associated with drainage? | regression | associational |
| Can we predict high-risk households? | prediction model | predictive |
| Does poor drainage cause water nuisance? | causal design needed | causal only with stronger assumptions |

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
The dataset does not decide the claim by itself. The design and assumptions do.
:::

## Outcome type guides the method

| Outcome type | Examples | Natural first methods |
|---|---|---|
| **Continuous** | income, score, biomass | means, linear regression |
| **Binary** | yes/no hypertension, dropout | proportions, logistic regression |
| **Categorical** | district, job sector | cross-tabs, multinomial models |
| **Ordinal** | low/middle/high, Likert | ordered comparisons, ordinal models |
| **Counts** | number of events | rates, count models |
| **Time series** | yearly revenues | trends, change, cautious models |
| **Measurement comparison** | ULS vs field inventory | agreement, calibration, prediction error |

## Continuous outcomes

Some outcomes are **continuous**: they can take many numerical values, and differences between values are meaningful. Examplesare:

- body mass index
- household income

For continuous outcomes, we often ask whether the **average level** differs between groups, or whether the outcome changes with another variable.

| Type of question | Example | What do we compare? | Appropriate first step |
|---|---|---|---|
| Describe one continuous outcome | Average math score | Mean, median and variation | Summary table and histogram |
| Compare two groups | Math score  | Difference in average score | Group means and boxplot |
| Compare more than two groups | Biomass by forest type or district | Differences between several group means | Grouped summary table |
| Study association  | Biomass and tree height | relation between values | Scatterplot |
| Adjust for background characteristics | Math score by language proficiency, accounting for household wealth and district | Difference after adjustment | Regression model |

## Possible methods for continuous outcomes

| Situation | Possible method |
|---|---|
| We want to summarize a continuous outcome | Mean, median, standard deviation, interquartile range |
| We want to visualize the distribution | Histogram, density plot or boxplot |
| We compare the average outcome between two groups | Difference in means or t-test |
| We compare the average outcome across several groups | ANOVA-style comparison or regression with group indicators |
| We study the association between two continuous variables | Scatterplot and correlation |
| We want to adjust for background variables | Linear regression |
| The outcome is very skewed, such as income | Consider median, transformation, robust summaries, or careful interpretation |

## Binary outcomes

Some outcomes have only **two possible values**. Examples are:

- hypertension: yes/no
- school dropout: yes/no
- trusts government: yes/no
- employed: yes/no

For binary outcomes, we often describe the **percentage** with the outcome in each group.

| Type of question | Example | What do we compare? | Appropriate first step |
|---|---|---|---|
| Describe one binary outcome | Percentage with hypertension | Proportion or percentage with “yes” | Frequency table |
| Compare two groups | Dropout by mother’s education | Difference in percentages | Cross-table |
| Compare risk between groups | Water nuisance in low/high-risk areas | Risk difference or risk ratio | Percentages per group |
| Study association with background variables | Hypertension by age, gender and lifestyle | Adjusted association | Logistic regression |
| Small groups or rare outcome | Dropout in small subgroups | Exact comparison | Fisher’s exact test |

## Possible methods for binary outcomes

| Situation | Possible method |
|---|---|
| We want to summarize a binary outcome | Percentage or proportion |
| We compare percentages between groups | Cross-table |
| We want an easily interpretable group difference | Risk difference |
| We want a relative comparison | Risk ratio |
| We model a binary outcome with predictors | Logistic regression |
| Groups are small or cells contain very few cases | Fisher's exact test |
| We report logistic regression | Translate odds or log-odds carefully into plain language |

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
# Interpretation trap

Odds are not probabilities.

If the probability of an event is 20%, the odds are 20 to 80, or 0.25.  
If the probability is 50%, the odds are 50 to 50, or 1.

An odds ratio can sound like a risk ratio, but it is not the same. For students and policy audiences, it is often clearer to also report predicted probabilities or percentages.
:::

## Categorical and ordinal outcomes

Some outcomes are **categories**: each observation belongs to one group or type.

Categorical examples:

- employment sector
- district
- type of schooling
- source of drinking water

Other outcomes are **ordered categories**: the values have a meaningful order, but the distance between categories is not necessarily equal.

Ordinal examples:

- low / middle / high trust
- strongly disagree → strongly agree
- poor / fair / good health
- no education / primary / secondary / tertiary education

## Categorical and ordinal outcomes
| Type of outcome | Example | What do we compare? | Appropriate description |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nominal categorical | Employment sector | Distribution across categories | Frequency table |
| Nominal categorical by group | Type of schooling by district | Whether category distributions differ across groups | Cross-table |
| Ordinal categorical | Low / middle / high trust | Ordered distribution of responses | Ordered frequency table |
| Ordinal categorical by group | Trust level by age group | Whether one group tends to score higher or lower | Grouped ordinal comparison |

## Possible methods for categorical outcomes {.scrollable}

| Situation | Possible method |
|---|---|
| We only want to summarize categories | Frequency table |
| We compare categories across groups | Cross-table |
| We test whether two categorical variables are associated | Chi-square test |
| We model an unordered categorical outcome with more than two categories | Multinomial logistic regression |
| We model an ordered categorical outcome | Ordinal logistic regression |
| The sample size is small or some cells are sparse | Simpler grouped comparisons or combine categories before analysis |

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
# Why not always use a complex model?

Categorical outcomes can quickly create many small groups.  
For example, five districts, three education levels and four age groups already create many combinations.

If many cells contain only a few observations, a complex model may become unstable or difficult to interpret. 

In that case, a simpler comparison, fewer categories, or a more descriptive analysis may give a more honest but equally informative answer.
:::

## Counts and rates
Some outcomes are **counts**: we count how often something happens.Examples:

- number of visits to a clinic
- number of flood events
- number of incidents in an area
- number of days absent from school

But a count is not always directly comparable. Sometimes we need to take into account the **exposure** or **opportunity** for something to happen.

| Question | Example | Appropriate description |
|---|---|---|
| How often does something happen? | Number of incidents per district | Count table |
| How often does something happen relatively? | Incidents per 10,000 inhabitants | Rate |
| How often does something happen per unit of time? | Clinic visits per month | Rate over time |
| How often does something happen per person, household, or area? | Absence days per student | Rate per unit |

## Possible methods {.scrollable}

| Situation | Possible method |
|---|---|
| We only want to summarize counts | Frequency table or count table |
| We compare counts between groups with equal exposure | Cross-table or simple group comparison |
| We compare counts between groups with different exposure | Rates, for example per inhabitant, household, month, or area |
| We model counts as an outcome | Poisson regression |
| The counts vary much more than a Poisson model expects | Negative binomial regression |

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
# Why negative binomial regression?
A Poisson model expects the average count and the spread of the counts to be roughly aligned.

If some areas or groups show much more variation than expected — for example many zeroes and a few extremely high counts — then a Poisson model may be too restrictive. This is called **overdispersion**.

In that case, negative binomial regression may be more appropriate because it allows for extra variation.
:::

## Time series and repeated measurements

Some outcomes are observed **over time** or **repeatedly for the same unit**. Examples:

- mining revenues from 2010–2025
- tax income per year
- yearly forest-cover change

The first step is usually not a model. The first step is to **draw the time pattern**.

| Type of question | Example | What do we compare? | Appropriate first step |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trend over time | Mining revenues from 2010–2025 | Do values increase, decrease, or fluctuate? | Line plot |
| Difference between periods | Tax income before and after a policy change | Are values different before and after a moment in time? | Before/after plot and descriptive comparison |
| Repeated measurements | Forest cover measured yearly in the same area | Does the same unit change over time? | Line plot per unit or area |
| Simple time association | Inflation by year | Is there a general linear trend? | Simple regression on time |

## Time series and repeated measurements

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
# Important question

Are we studying **change over time**, or are we comparing **independent groups**?

For example:

- tax income in Suriname from 2010–2025  
- tax income in different districts in one year  

These require different ways of thinking about the data.
:::

## Possible methods for time series

| Situation | Possible method |
|---|---|
| We want to describe change over time | Line plot and descriptive trend comparison |
| We compare two broad periods | Before/after comparison, with caution |
| We want to estimate a simple trend | Regression with time as predictor |
| We have repeated observations within the same unit | Repeated-measures or panel-style approach |
| We have only 10–15 yearly observations | Keep the analysis simple and avoid overfitting |
| There may be a policy change or shock | Show the timing clearly and interpret cautiously |

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
# Small-N warning

A complex time-series model is rarely convincing with 10–15 yearly observations.

With few years, the model can easily start describing random fluctuations instead of a real pattern. A clear figure, a simple trend description, and careful language are often stronger.
:::

## Measurement and validation questions

Sometimes the research question is not about explaining an outcome, but about **checking whether a measurement is good enough**. Examples:

- Does a short test measure the same construct as a longer test?
- Do administrative records agree with survey responses?
- Does a new indicator classify households similarly to an existing measure?

| Validation question | Example | What do we compare? | Appropriate first step |
|---|---|---|---|
| Agreement between two measurements | ULS biomass estimate vs forest inventory biomass | Do both methods give similar values? | Scatterplot against reference measurement |
| Accuracy of a new measure | Short test vs long test | How far are the new measurements from the reference? | Mean error, MAE, RMSE |
| Consistency of classification | Administrative poverty status vs survey poverty status | Do both sources classify units similarly? | Cross-table |
| Systematic bias | New sensor vs field measurement | Is the new method systematically too high or too low? | Difference plot or Bland-Altman style plot |

## Possible methods

| Situation | Possible method |
|---|---|
| We want a first visual check | Scatterplot against reference measurement |
| We want to know whether two measures move together | Correlation |
| We want to quantify average error | Mean error |
| We want to quantify typical absolute error | Mean absolute error, MAE |
| We want to penalize larger errors more strongly | Root mean squared error, RMSE |
| We want to inspect agreement and bias | Bland-Altman style agreement plot |
| We want to adjust or translate one measurement into another | Calibration model |

## Covariates: make comparisons fairer
A covariate is a variable we include because it helps us make a comparison more meaningful, more precise, or less misleading.

| Job of a covariate | What it means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Reduce confounding | We compare groups that differ in other important ways | Compare dropout by mother’s education while also considering household wealth |
| Improve precision | We explain some background variation, so the main comparison becomes clearer | Include child’s age when comparing school performance |
| Compare like with like | We avoid comparing very different units as if they were the same | Compare districts while accounting for urban/rural composition |
| Account for design differences | We respect how the data were collected | Include survey weights, clusters, or strata where relevant |
| Avoid misleading group comparisons | We prevent a crude comparison from carrying too much weight | Compare clinic visits while accounting for population size or access to care |

## Covariates make comparisons fairer
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
# Example

If we compare dropout by mother’s education, should we also consider household wealth, district, child's age and school attendance?

Without these background variables, the comparison may partly reflect other differences between households rather than mother’s education alone.
:::

## Covariates in an analysis plan

| Analysis question | Possible covariates | Why they may matter |
|---|---|---|
| Is language skill associated with math performance? | Age, district, school attendance, household wealth | These factors may affect both language skill and math performance |
| Does trust in government differ by age group? | Education, district, employment status | Age groups may differ in social and economic background |
| Are flood reports higher in some districts? | Population size, urban/rural area, drainage access | Districts differ in exposure and infrastructure |
| Is health-care use associated with income? | Age, gender, distance to clinic, insurance status | Health-care use also depends on need and access |

## Choosing background variables

Good covariate choices usually come from the research design, not from searching for the model that gives the nicest result.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
# Important question

Why is this variable in the model?

A covariate should have a clear function. If we cannot explain why it is included, it probably does not belong in the analysis plan yet.
:::

## Poor covariate choices

| Poor strategy | Why it is risky | Better alternative |
|---|---|---|
| Include everything available | The model may become unstable or hard to interpret | Select variables based on literature, theory and design |
| Include only significant variables | This turns model building into result hunting | Decide key covariates before looking at results |
| Add or remove variables until the result looks good | This can produce misleading conclusions | Report a planned main model and simple robustness checks |
| Control for variables that are consequences of the exposure | This may remove part of the effect or change the question | Think carefully about the causal or conceptual order |
| Use covariates without understanding them | Administrative variables may not mean what we think | Check codebooks and definitions |

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
# A covariate can change the question

For example:

- Crude question: Do children from different wealth groups differ in school performance?
- Adjusted question: Do children from different wealth groups differ in school performance, among children with similar age, district and school attendance?

Both questions can be useful, but they are not the same question.
:::

## A practical model map

| Research situation | Start simple | Model option |
|---|---|---|
| Mean score differs by group | group means + CI | linear regression, t-test, ANOVA |
| Yes/no outcome differs by group | percentages, tables | logistic regression |
| Association between two continuous variables | scatterplot, correlation | linear regression |
| Several groups, categorical outcome | cross-tab | multinomial model |
| Outcome over years | line plot | simple trend model |
| Measurement A vs measurement B | scatterplot + error | agreement/calibration |

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Start with the simplest analysis that directly answers the comparison.
:::

## Diagnostics: what can go wrong?

Diagnostics are not only technical.

They answer practical questions:

- Do we have enough observations?
- Are groups large enough?
- Are there many missing values?
- Are there extreme values?
- Is the model dominated by one subgroup?
- Are assumptions roughly plausible?
- Does the output make substantive sense?

## Model-specific checks

| Method | Simple checks |
|---|---|
| group comparison | group sizes and variances, missing values, outliers |
| linear regression | residuals, influential cases, linearity, normality of errors |
| logistic regression | events per variable, separation, predicted probabilities |
| chi-square test | expected cell counts |
| time trend | plot over time, influential years, definition changes |
| prediction model | train/test split or cross-validation when possible |

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
Do not report a model you cannot explain to someone else!.
:::

## Interpretation before p-values

Statistical output is not yet an answer. Ask yourselves:

1. What was compared?
2. What is the direction of the result?
3. How large is the difference or association?
4. How uncertain is it?
5. Is the result meaningful in context?
6. Is the claim not too strong?

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
# A good result flow
Estimate → uncertainty → interpretation → limitation.
:::

## From method to table or figure

The table or figure should make the comparison visible.

| Question | Useful display |
|---|---|
| How common is X? | bar chart, frequency table |
| Do groups differ? | grouped bar chart, dot plot with intervals |
| Is X related to Y? | scatterplot, coefficient plot |
| Is there a trend? | line plot |
| Does a model predict well? | observed vs predicted, error plot |
| Do measures agree? | agreement plot, residual/error plot |

## Now the second layer: robustness
A conclusion is more credible when it does not disappear under reasonable alternative choices.

Robustness is not about proving we are right. It is about asking:

> How fragile is my answer?

If a reasonable alternative choice changes the answer, we need to report that fragility.

## Uncertainty is broader than p-values

Uncertainty can enter through:

- sampling
- measurement
- missing data
- coding and cleaning decisions
- model choice
- covariate choice
- time period choice
- subgroup definitions
- external validity

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
Remember: A narrow confidence interval around the wrong target is still wrong!
:::

## Assumptions connect analysis to claim

| Assumption | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| representative sample | can we generalize? |
| valid measurement | are variables measuring the intended concepts? |
| no major omitted confounders | is the comparison fair? |
| stable definitions | can periods or groups be compared? |
| sufficient sample size | is the result too noisy? |
| missingness not too harmful | are observed cases informative? |
| model form adequate | does the model capture the comparison? |

## Threats to validity

Common threats in applied projects:

- selection bias
- confounding
- reverse causality
- nonresponse
- measurement error
- changing definitions over time
- small subgroups
- outliers
- inaccessible raw data
- hidden populations

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
# Good practice
Identify and discuss the threat before your colleague, supervisor or any other reader does!
:::

## A menu of easy robustness checks

| Concern | Easy check |
|---|---|
| coding choice | try an alternative coding |
| questionable variable | run with and without it |
| outliers | compare with and without extreme cases, give outliers less weight |
| missing data | compare complete cases with broader sample, change the imputations if you suspect a direction |
| survey weights | compare weighted and unweighted results |
| subgroup dominance | repeat/stratified analysis by subgroup |
| model complexity | compare complex model with simple model |
| time aggregation | inspect results by year and compare to the overall measure|

## Example 1: comparing groups over years

Suppose we compare average income between two groups over 2018–2024.

A weak check:

> Group A has a higher average than Group B over all years combined.

A better robustness check:

> Does Group A have a higher average in each separate year?

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
# Practical check
Make one table with group means per year, or one line plot per group.
:::

## Example 1: what could happen?

| Pattern | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| difference appears in every year | more robust descriptive pattern |
| difference appears only in one year | result may be driven by that year |
| difference changes direction | average hides instability |
| one year has very small N | result may be unreliable |
| definitions changed in one year | trend may not be comparable |

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
Pooling years can make a pattern look stable even when it is not.
:::

## Example 2: binary outcome

Research question:

> Is hypertension more common among workers with a certain lifestyle factor?

Primary analysis:

- percentage hypertensive by lifestyle group
- logistic regression adjusted for age and sex

Robustness checks:

- compare crude and adjusted results
- add ethnicity or occupation if justified
- inspect results by age group
- check whether small groups drive the result

## Example 3: missing values

Suppose a key covariate has many missing values.

Possible checks:

- compare complete cases with the full available sample
- compare people with and without missingness on observed variables
- run a simpler model without the covariate
- report how much the sample size changes

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
# Missing data questions
1. Who disappears from the analysis when we require complete data?

2. Do the results change when different samples/models are used?
:::
